characterizations.result_summary: No new peaks were observed in the IR spectra of the polymer blends, all detected peaks correspond to the characteristic IR bands of the base polymers PCL, PDLLA and PLGA.

DSC analysis was conducted to determine Tg, Tm and crystallinity of base polymers and blends; PDLLA/PLGA blends showed single Tg indicating miscibility, while Tg of PDLLA and PLGA in PCL-containing blends was masked by PCL's Tm, and crystallinity of PCL decreased with increasing PDLLA/PLGA content.

Initial trials were carried out using several commonly used solvents, e.g., dichloromethane, chloroform, tetrahydrofuran and ethyl acetate, in an attempt to determine the most suitable solvent to dissolve PLGA, PCL and PDLLA.
Acetone was chosen as it partially dissolves PLGA, PDLLA and PCL at room temperature and requires only gentle heating to fully dissolve the polymers<sup>[10,13,14]</sup>.

In this study, the IR peaks for the compression moulded PCL, PDLLA and PLGA samples were in good agreement with the characteristic bands reported by Coleman and Zarian (1979), Garlotta (2001), Vey et al.
A representative infrared spectrum of one of the compression moulded thin film blends (PCL 50% PDLLA=50% PCL) is presented in Figure 1.

DSC was used to analyse the effect that blending of the polymers had on the endothermic $( T _ { g }$and $T _ { m } )$peaks of the constituent polymers and to assess what impact blending PDLLA and PLGA with PCL had on the crystallinity of the samples.
The DSC thermographs of PDLLA, PLGA and 50%PDLLA=50%PLGA are shown in Figure 2.
In Figure 3, the thermographs of the 80%PDLLA= 20%PLGA, 50%PDLLA=50%PLGA and 20%PDLLA= 80%PLGA blends are presented.
Phase separation of binary blends of PLA and PLGA is not as likely as with many other polymer combinations due to their similarity in chemical structure<sup>[20]</sup>.
The $T _ { m }$of PLGA is not visible in the 50% and 80% blends of PDLLA with PLGA.

(2008) whom found there was a reduction in crystallinity in PLGA=PLA blends (with increasing PLA content) when blended as microparticles using solution-enhanced dispersion by supercritical fluids<sup>[22]</sup>.
DSC thermographs of compression moulded PCL homopolymer, and 50%PDLLA= 50%PCL and 50%PLGA=50%PCL blends are shown in Figure 4.
The percentage crystallinity of PCL is one of the most important properties controlling the degradation rate and the physical strength of the polymer<sup>[26]</sup>.

Regularity in its molecular structure renders Poly (e-caprolactone) highly crystallisable and in its usual state it is approximately 50% crystalline depending on molecular weight and processing conditions<sup>[28,29]</sup>.
Figure 4 demonstrates the effect of blending PCL with PLGA and PCL with PDLLA (blend ratio 50:50) on the crystalline peak.
There was a similar decrease in the calculated percentage crystallinity in PLGA=PCL samples, based on the same blend ratios.
Phosphate buffer solution (PBS) adsorption studies were carried out on thin film samples of PLGA, PCL, PDLLA and blends of these polymers.
In this study, the polymers PCL and PLGA are both semi-crystalline, which mainly accounts for their low percentage PBS uptakes.
The PBS adsorption of thin film blends of PDLLA=PCL is illustrated in Figure 6.
There is a considerably higher level of percentage PBS uptake in the 50%PDLLA= 50%PCL and 80%PDLLA=20%PCL blends, than in the PCL and the 20%PDLLA=80%PCL samples.

The increase in level of PBS uptake in the PCL=PDLLA blends at higher PDLLA contents is most likely a consequence of the reduction in crystallinity, as detailed in the previous section, thus the higher percentage of amorphous polymer present in the samples is likely to be responsible for this trend.
The PBS adsorptions of the thin film blends of PLGA= PCL were also analysed.
Finally, the PBS adsorption of thin film PDLLA=PLGA blends was examined as shown in Figure 7.

In Figures 8 and 9, the tensile strength and Young’s modulus of PLGA=PCL and PDLLA=PCL are plotted across the composition range.

Presented in Figures 10 and 11, the tensile strength and Young’s Modulus of blends of PDLLA=PLGA are plotted across the entire composition range.

There is some evidence of miscibility between the blends, as the sample of 50%PDLLA=50%PLGA has a Young’s Modulus greater than values obtained for PLGA or PDLLA, and the corresponding tensile strength is greater than the values obtained for PDLLA.
The 20%PDLLA=80%PLGA blend has a higher tensile strength than the PDLLA but lower than PLGA.

The changes in tensile properties of the thin film PDLLA=PLGA blends could also be related to dense chain packing in the amorphous regions due to a strong interaction between the l- and d-unit sequences, which is dependent on the polymer-mixing ratio<sup>[30]</sup>.
The 80%PDLLA= 20%PLGA blend shows a decrease in tensile strength when compared to the PLGA or PDLLA.

Also some miscible polymer blends of PLA and their copolymers with other polymers have become immiscible as the molecular weight increased because of the decreased polarity of polymer chains and the entropy of mixing<sup>[38]</sup>.

A two-step procedure was developed for the solvent casting of the thin films.

The first step involved dissolving the polymer or polymer mixtures; $5 \mathrm { g }$of the polymer or polymer mixtures were weighed and placed into a glass beaker, 50 ml of chloroform was added and the polymer=solvent mixture was agitated using a magnetic stirrer for a period of between 2–4 hr until the polymers were fully dissolved.

Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis was carried out using a Perkin-Elmer, Pyris 6 DSC. Samples of between 9.3–10.3 mg were prepared from the base polymers and polymer blends. All measurements were conducted in crimped non-hermetic aluminium pans with an empty crimped aluminium pan being used as the reference cell. To assess the melting points and miscibility of the polymer(s), the samples were heated from a temperature of 20 °C to 200 °C at a rate of 10 °C per minute. All DSC tests were carried out under a 20 ml/min flow of nitrogen to prevent oxidation.

The testing procedure for the phosphate buffered saline (PBS) adsorption was based on ASTM international standard D570-81 standard test method for water adsorption of plastics. Three samples of each batch were cut into 60 mm by 10 mm strips and placed in test-tubes and dried in an oven for 24 hr at a temperature of 50 °C. Samples were immersed in PBS at a temperature of 50 °C.

The tensile testing procedure used was based on the ASTM international standard D882-02 standard test method for tensile properties of thin plastic sheeting. The samples were cut into tensile samples using a dumbbell cutter, which gave a sample test length of 20 mm and a width of 4 mm. Five samples were tested from each batch using a Lloyd Lrx Tensile tester, with Nexygen software. A cross-head speed of 20 mm/min was used during all tests.
The contact angles of water on the thin film polymers were measured using a Rame-Hart Goniometer at room temperature (20 °C). The drops were made using a Gilson Pipetman set to 0.1 ml.

In the 50% blend of the two polymers, a single $T _ { g }$was evident at $5 4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$
The percentage crystallinity calculated for compression moulded PCL homopolymer was 53.5%.

The percentage PBS uptake of the PLGA films proved similar to work carried out by Loo et al. (2005), with the films exhibiting a PBS uptake of less than 2 wt% after 120 hr

Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy
Attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) was carried out on rectangular samples using a Nicolet Avator 360 FTIR, with a 32 scan per sample cycle.
Infrared Spectroscopy of Thin Film Polymer Blends

In this study, the IR peaks for the compression moulded PCL, PDLLA and PLGA samples were in good agreement with the characteristic bands reported by Coleman and Zarian (1979), Garlotta (2001), Vey et al. (2008) and Choi et al. (2008) for these homopolymers<sup>[15–18]</sup>.
Throughout this study, there were no peaks present in the IR spectra of the blends that could not be explained by the characteristic IR bands of the base polymers.
Differential Scanning Calorimetry

Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis was carried out using a Perkin-Elmer, Pyris 6 DSC. Samples of between 9.3–10.3 mg were prepared from the base polymers and polymer blends. All measurements were conducted in crimped non-hermetic aluminium pans with an empty crimped aluminium pan being used as the reference cell. To assess the melting points and miscibility of the polymer(s), the samples were heated from a temperature of $2 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$to $2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$at a rate of $1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$per minute. For investigation of the crystalline interactions, samples were heated from a temperature of $2 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$to $2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$at a rate of $1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C }$per minute and held isothermal for a 5-min period. The samples were then cooled down from 200<sup></sup>C to 20<sup></sup>C at a rate of 2<sup></sup>C per minute. All DSC tests were carried out under a 20 ml=min flow of nitrogen to prevent oxidation. High-purity indium was used to calibrate the DSC cell.
